3-4: A statement no islander can ever make, such as 'I am a liar'.
One islander speaks about himself and another together: 'we are both liars', or 'at least one of us is a liar'.
A chain or a row of islanders, each saying the next one, or the one in front, is a liar: how many knights.
Three islanders, each saying how many liars there are among the three.
A round table where everyone says a neighbour is a liar: how many knights can sit there.
What one islander said, as another reports it: whether the report can be true, and who each of them is.
An islander asked whether another is a knight: what the answer tells about each of them.
Two islanders saying the same sentence, and what follows for both of them.
'Ben and I are of the same kind' said by one of two islanders: what it shows about the other.
A sentence about a plain fact, such as a sum or the days of a week, that sorts the speakers into knights and liars.
Suspects who each say who did it, with how many of them tell the truth known, such as only the guilty one: try each suspect as the guilty one and count the true sentences.
Creatures that lie about one thing only, such as their own gold, and tell the truth about all else: what a sentence is about decides whether it can be false.
Two claims of which one follows from the other, such as 'older than eleven' and 'older than ten', with exactly one of them wrong: the stronger claim is the wrong one.
Everyone in a group saying 'all the rest of you are liars': two knights would call each other liars, and if all were liars each would be right, so exactly one is a knight.
Two islanders who say opposite things, such as 'it rained' and 'it did not rain': one of them is a knight and the other a liar.
Creatures whose number of legs or spots says whether they tell the truth, speaking of those numbers: what each says must fit the kind its own number makes it.
5-6: Several islanders each saying how many knights there are, every number different.
What another islander would answer if asked: a statement about a statement.
A circle where each says both neighbours are liars: the fewest and the most knights possible.
A third kind of islander, who lies and tells the truth in turn.
'Exactly one of us is a knight' said by several islanders at once.
A question to which every islander, knight or liar, gives the same answer.
Statements joined by 'or' and 'and', such as 'I am a liar or Ben is a knight'.
A row of islanders, each saying how many liars stand to the left of them.
The fewest questions that tell the knights from the liars among a few islanders.
'Most of us are liars' said by some of the islanders in a group: how many knights the group can have.
Islanders who each support one of three or more teams, asked about every team: a knight says yes once and a liar to every team but its own, so the yeses count the knights.
Islanders who each think of a number and say in two sentences that it is more than one value and less than another: a liar's number fits neither, so its second value is at most its first.
Islanders in pairs, each calling the other a knight or a liar: two of a kind both say 'knight', and a knight with a liar both say 'liar', so 'liar' is said in twos.
Someone who lies on some days of the week and tells the truth on the others: a sentence about yesterday or tomorrow can be said only on the days it fits.
People who tell the truth to their own side and lie to the other, such as two firms or two teams: a sentence is true just when the one who says it and the one who hears it are on one side.
